title: Al-Hayy, the Ever-Living
tomorrow: the verse says He never sleeps. why would that help us sleep?

lines: STAY STRONG, OR LET IT OUT?
ALLAH IS ALIVE AND DOES NOT DIE.
cards: Grief advice splits in two. One side says stay strong, they're in a better place. The other says let it out, cry as long as you need.
The day the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, died, Medina heard something like both. Umar, the reports say, couldn't accept it.
Then Abu Bakr stood and said: whoever worshiped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worships Allah, Allah is alive and does not die.
And he recited, in Pickthall's words: "Muhammad is but a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) have passed away before him."

teach.h: THE ALIVE. NO SLUMBER, NO SLEEP.
teach.b: Today's Name is Al-Hayy, the Ever-Living. Ayat al-Kursi says it plainly: "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him."
So how should someone grieve, if the One they hold to never dies? Two views live inside the tradition, and each has a real case. The first says steadiness.
Abu Bakr's sentence held a whole city upright on its worst day.
Its best case: grief that forgets the Ever-Living can swallow a person whole, and remembering that He remains is what lets you stand at a grave and still walk home. The second says tears.
When the Prophet's baby son, Ibrahim, was dying, the Prophet wept. Someone was surprised, and he said: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord.
Its best case: if the Prophet cried, tears can't be a failure of faith; they're mercy.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in the hadith, the Prophet sets the tears and the faith side by side in one sentence, and neither cancels the other.
The tears belong to the one who died. The steadiness belongs to the One who doesn't.

how: Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi (2:255), which names Allah the Ever-Living, after prayers and before sleep, and call on Him as 'Ya Hayyu ya Qayyum' in hard moments.

o: the Living Spirit inside each creature
the Eternal Judge who outlasts the world
the Ever-Living, whose life never sleeps

games.q: the hardest day — tap the pairs.
p: Allah is alive and does not die

s: the Prophet never wept at a death, to show strong faith
he wept for his son Ibrahim: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves.
Ayat al-Kursi says neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Allah

games.q: you lean toward 'let the tears come.' your friend leans toward 'stay steady.' the teacher asks you to give HER side's best case. which do you give?
o: steadiness is just a polite way of hiding feelings.
Abu Bakr's 'Allah is alive and does not die' held a grieving city upright.
crying is weakness, and faith should never look weak.
games.why: the strongest case for steadiness is Abu Bakr on the worst day: remembering the Ever-Living let people stand. the Prophet's tears are the other side's best case, and both are in the tradition.

practice: Sit still and find your pulse, at your wrist or your neck, or simply listen to your breathing. That small rhythm keeps going without being asked.
For the two minutes, let it point past itself to the life that never sleeps, and just keep it company.

wordCard.voice: Al-Hayy. The Ever-Living: the Alive, whom neither slumber nor sleep overtakes, still here on the hardest day.

orig.note: Arabic: the Ever-Living. Ayat al-Kursi pairs it with Al-Qayyum, tomorrow's Name; Pickthall: 'the Alive, the Eternal'.

carryVoice: Your line: ever-living, the One who is still here when the tears come. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him.
Muhammad is but a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) have passed away before him.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3667–3668 (Abu Bakr: whoever worshiped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; Allah is alive and does not die)
